body.head: CONDITIONAL SENTENCES IN BIBLICAL HEBREW PROSE 1283
body.p: 4.3 The use of כי and אם typical in this pattern does not differ from the standard use described in #2 and #3. Since the clause introduced by כי is not hypothetical, but presents an event expected to occur, a statement clause with a participle or with אשר as subject of a verb ('The one who does...') may be used in parallel with a clause introduced by כי ('When a person does ...'). For examples see Exod 21:12-17, also Lev 5:1-4 discussed in #6.1. The אם clauses introduce possible variants on or alternatives to the preceding כי clause, a typical function of אם. אם clauses are used after laws with other forms of introduction, in just the same way as they are after כי clauses. Examples occur in Exodus 22:21 (22, 24, 25);The אם clauses in verses 24 and 25 introduce new types of 'underprivileged' to whom consideration must be shown. They are related to the preceding only through the 2m.s pronoun in the verb form, that is, more loosely than usual. Leviticus 7:11 (12, 16, 18); 20:2 (4); Numbers 35:25 (26); Deuteronomy 22:1 (2); 30:16 (17).
body.head: 5 Minor Irregularities in the Pattern
body.p: 5.1 In Leviticus 1, the pattern dependent on the כי clause in Lev 1:2 is continued in the אם clauses in chapter 3. The material in chapter two disrupts it. In Leviticus 27, the last three אם clauses (Lev 27:27, 27, 31) appear to continue the pattern de-
1284 E.J. REVELL
pendent on the כי clause in 27:2. The pattern initiated by the כי clause in 27:14 disrupts it.

5.2 In Leviticus 4, three אם clauses which follow the initial כי clause (and further restrict it, as in Exod 22:6-7, see #4.1) do not contain anaphora, since each introduces a new class of sinner. (There is a similar example in Num 15:27.) In Lev 4:22, a clause introducing a further class of sinner ( a ‘leader’) is placed between the second and third אם clause, disrupting the pattern. This clause is introduced by אשר, a common particle not elsewhere equivalent to אם (see #8.2).
body.head: 6 Exceptional uses of כי and אם
body.p: 6.1 או כי ‘Or when’ is sometimes used to introduce alternative protases with the same apodosis (alternative situations for which the judgment is the same: Exod 21:33, Lev 15:25, and Deut 24:312.). An extension of this usage occurs in the beginning of Leviticus 5. Here four different situations are presented with different introductions. ... ונפש כי תחטא ‘When a person sins...’ (Lev 5:1), או נפש ... אשר תגע ‘Or a person who touches...’ (5:2), ... או כי יגע ‘Or when he touches...’ (5:3), ... או נפש כי תשבע ‘Or when a person swears...’ (5:4). These four situations are then summarized in a further כי clause, which introduces the description of the procedure to be followed in all of them: ... יאשם לאחת מאלה והיה כי ‘When he is guilty through any of these...’ (Lev 5:5). In Lev 5:23 ... יחטא והיה כי ‘When he sins...’ begins a similar sentence summarizing a set of alternatives introduced by או which are placed within the כי clause of 5:21. The atypical lack of nominal subject in these כי clauses in Lev 5:5 and 5:21 reflects their relationship to what precedes.
body.note: In Deut 24:3b, ... או כי ימות ‘Or if he dies...’ ‘he’ is the second husband, so this clause, although alternative specifically only to ... ושנאה האיש ... וכתב ‘The man dislikes her..., and divorces her...’ in 24:3a, assumes the preceding material (24:1-2) which is introduced by כי. או כי ‘Or’ is more commonly used to give alternatives within a protasis: introduced by כי in Num 5:14, 30:3, or by אם in Num 30:11, 35:20, or to give alternatives within an apodosis, as in Lev 25:49, Num 15:6.
body.head: CONDITIONAL SENTENCES IN BIBLICAL HEBREW PROSE 1285
body.p: 6.2 In Lev 13:16, או כי ‘Or when’ introduces an alternative symptom, where ואם ‘and if’ is certainly to be expected. כי (ו) ‘(And) when’ is used in a similar way in Lev 11:37, 38, Num 6:9 and Deut 15:21, as is והיה כי in Deut 15:16.13 All these כי clauses include anaphora. In Deut 23:11, 23, 25, 26, where כי (ו) might also be held to introduce an alternative, the only anaphora are pronouns representing the person addressed. Consequently these examples of כי can be taken as introducing new topics.

6.3 Num 5:20 ... ואת כי שטית ... וכי נטמאת, is usually translated as conditional ‘But if you have gone astray... and become unclean...’. כי would then introduce the second of two mutually exclusive alternatives where the first is introduced by אם (Num 5:19), a phenomenon without parallel. The use of כי with a perfect verb is unexpected, and the relation of this verse to its context is not clear. Consequently the function of כי here must be regarded as uncertain.

6.4 Temporal/conditional כי went out of use over the biblical period. It is not found in Qohelet, Esther, Daniel, Ezra, or Nehemiah, or in Chronicles outside parallels to Samuel-Kings. The occasional use of אם in these books where ‘when’ would be appropriate reflects its progressive disuse, (as Qoh 4:11, 5:7, 2 Chron 6:22, 24, 20:9). This late tendency to use אם instead of כי may account for the use of both (where only one is required) in ... ואם נפש כי (Lev 5:17). The clause is without anaphora, so אם is most probably secondary. In ... כי אם צעק יצעק (Exod 22:22), כי אם must either give a strong positive emphasis (as Jud 15:7), or result from error. The outcry of the oppressed is certainly expected, so כי alone should be used, as in Exod 22:26 etc.14
body.note: 13 אם is used in the similar context in Exod 21:5. The כי clause in Deut 15:12 begins this section. That in 15:13 (which includes anaphora) describes an act required by 15:12, so that introductory אם would not be appropriate.

14 אם replaces biblical כי in some Qumran scrolls: 4Q158:10-12:4 (Exod 21:37. In line 3, אם also replaces the surprising או beginning 21:36) and in the Temple Scroll 53:12, 55:2, 13, 15, 61:7 (Deut 23:23, 13:13, 19, 17:2, 19:16). וכי אם תדור in 53:11 (כי תדר Deut 23:22) is presumably a doublet (as Lev 5:17), possibly also the non-biblical וכי אם תחזק (58:10). Temporal/conditional כי is unchanged in 12 other biblical examples, and is also used in 50:10, 58:3 and 64:6. Beyond 1QS 5:20, 6:4, I have not noticed sure cases in other non-biblical materials. כי is used in the Samaritan Pentateuch as in the Masoretic. In the Mishna, it is virtually restricted to an interrogative function, reflecting a development different from the biblical.
body.p: 6.5 The use of כי can be justified in the other cases I have noted in which אם might seem more appropriate. Thus the negative tone of Jos 24:19 ‘You are unable to serve the Lord’ justifies the otherwise surprising expectation expressed by ... כי תעזבר ‘When you forsake Yahweh...’ in 24:20. In Num 10:29, Moses invites Hobab to accompany Israel. He refuses. The request is renewed. ... כי תלך ‘When you come’ (10:32) gives positive support to this second request by presenting Hobab’s agreement as expected. (The text suggests that Hobab did go, but this is not clear.)
body.head: 7 Semantic Overlap of כי and אם
body.p: 7.1 The use of כי in the examples in #6.1-3 could be held to show that כי was synonymous with אם. However, the two particles are typically used distinctly, and could well have different values even where they appear to be used in the same situation. For example, both particles introduce subordinate clauses with a second person imperfect form of שמע before or after the main clause. אם in a preceding clause presents an unpredictable personal reaction (#3.3) "If you do/do not listen to/obey..." (Gen 34:17, and 10 cases concerned with obedience to God). כי in this position presents an expected event "When you hear news..." (Deut 13:13). Following the main clause, the limiting effect of an אם clause is stressed (and, in Deut 15:5, emphasized by רק) "(God will bless you) only if you obey." A כי clause in this position stresses the factual relationship as Deut 28:1-2 "If (אם) you obey... all these blessings will come to you... because (כי) you obey..." (also Deut 13:19, 28:13, 30:10).

7.2 It seems evident that one of the factors conditioning the choice of language even in the laws was a concern to avoid monotony (cf. #6.1 on Lev 5:1-4). If so, literary considerations may well have governed the choice of כי or אם where either might be used. Thus ... וכי יטהר ‘When he becomes clean...’ is used of the cure of a man who had a discharge, but ... ואם טהרה ‘If she has become
body.note: Aejmelaeus (1986:207) notes the common conditional or temporal rendering of כי clauses of this type, but adds that they ‘can usually be understood as causal or object clauses as well’. Van Leeuwen 1973:18, regards the כי clause in Deut 28:13 as equivalent to the אם clause in 28:1. However, this אם clause forms a contrasting pair (#3.1) with that in 28:15, and it is unlikely that the intervening כי clauses (28:2, 9, 13) disrupt this structure.

The use of אם is probably justified by the difference of temporal viewpoint, but it may also be intended to stress the difference between this case, which deals with an abnormal discharge (v. 25), from that of normal menstruation, where כי would be appropriate, as its termination is expected.

7.3 אם is occasionally used of events known to have happened in the past (where כאשר ‘when’ is expected). This may be intended to emphasize the idea of contingency. It would, then, have a meaning such as ‘If it did so happen’ -- that Onan visited his brother’s wife (Gen 38:9), -- that a snake bit (Num 21:9), -- that Israel sowed grain (Judg 6:3). Similarly, where אם introduces events true in the present (or past events relevant to it), it may be used (with various purposes) to suggest doubt of the fact, with a meaning such as ‘If it is really true that’ -- there is no money (Gen 47:16), a tribe is large (Jos 17:15), a runner is alone (2 Sam 18:25). Also Num 22:20, 1 Sam 15:17, 23:23.Also 2 Kgs 1:10, 12, unless אם is required by the conditional request form used. אם could be translated ‘since’ in some of these cases, but they do not differ from the others in form, and so presumably not in meaning. אם may similarly be used rhetorically of the certain future. In ‘If (אם) a Jubilee year should come...’ (Num 36:4), the context, a polite complaint against an existing law, justifies the tentative nature of the sentence. In ‘If (אם) the women should come out to dance’ (Jud 21:21), the use of אם, which marks as hypothetical an event essential to the elders’ kidnap plan, suggests that Providence, not the elders, will be responsible if an act which they would normally condemn succeeds.In Deut 19:8, the uncertainty of ‘If (אם) God should enlarge your boundaries’ is presumably justified by the limitation given in the following כי clause ‘Because/when you keep all these commandments’. Such obedience is not certain (cf. #7.1).

7.4 The semantic domains of כי and אם certainly overlap to the extent that, in some situations, either might be used. However, it is probable that each carried different implications, although no doubt (as with "when" and "if") the difference was not always important.

8 Other Types of Sentence Called ‘Conditional’
body.p: 8.1 Sentences introduced by לוּ / אִלּוּ and לוּלֵי As is well known, these particles show that the relationship suggested by the sentence is not valid; the protasis does not condition the apodosis. לוּלֵי is used to introduce a protasis which is factual; לוּ to introduce one that is not. אִלּוּ (Qoh 6:6, Esth 7:4) replaced לוּ by the end of the biblical period.

8.2 אֲשֶׁר as a Conditional Particle In most cases where a conditional value is suggested for אֲשֶׁר, it can equally well be understood in one of its more common values, e.g. as a relative particle in 1 Kgs 8:30 (cf. 8:28, 29). In Deut 11:13, 22, an אִם clause initiates a promise that obedience will be rewarded by the advantages referred to as the ‘blessing’ in 11:27. The first אֲשֶׁר in that verse expresses purpose (Cf. Gen 11:7, Deut 4:10, 6:3); God sets out the blessing ‘So that you will obey’. The אִם clause in 11:28 presents a contrasting alternative (see #3.2). No common use of אֲשֶׁר can be invoked in Lev 4:22, where אִם is expected (see #5.2), or in Num 5:29, Jos 4:21, where כִּי is expected. However, a larger number of examples, or some indication as to why such a rare value of such a common particle should be used in these particular cases, is needed to establish a conditional value for אֲשֶׁר as more than a possibility.

8.3 Asyndeton Conditional Sentences Other pairs of clauses may be translated by an English conditional sentence, as וְהִנֵּה נֵלֵךְ וּמַה נָּבִיא לָאִישׁ ‘If we go, what will we bring to the man?’ (1 Sam 9:7), ... וְצָמִת וְהָלַכְתְּ ... וְשָׁתִית ‘If you are thirsty, go... and drink...’ (Ruth 2:9). However, such cases can be treated, at least colloquially, in other ways. ‘So we go! What will we take the man?’ ‘You’re going to be thirsty. You can go... and drink...’ Where translation as a conditional is suitable (which is not true for all similar pairs), the protasis represents a known or accepted fact, a ‘given’. Similarly, זֹאת עֲשׂוּ וִחְיוּ (Gen 42:18, with imperative verbs) can be translated ‘If you do this you will live’, but its real meaning is much more positive. In 1 Kgs 21:2 ‘Give me (imperative) your vineyard... and I will give...’ could equally well be translated ‘If you give me... I will give...’, but this is a demand, and quite different from the mere offer of alternative compensation presented in the following אִם clause ‘Or if you like...’ (with adjective or stative verb cf. 21:6). The particles discussed above are

Where such a particle is not used, the basic relationship of the two clauses (the one contingent on the other), may well justify translation as a conditional sentence. However, if a translation ignores the difference in the surface structures, it loses part of the meaning of the Hebrew.
body.head: 9 Conclusion
body.p: 9.1 The types of conditional sentence discussed above can be divided into two categories: those in which the condition presented by the protasis is hypothetical, and those in which it is actual. Each can be further subdivided: under hypothetical, the condition may be invalid (it cannot occur), or it may be potential (its validity is not known). Under actual, the condition may impose a temporal restriction on the apodosis, or it may not impose any restriction at all. This can be illustrated by the following table.

The occasional use of כי where אם is expected (#6.2), and the fact that אם is (comparatively) rare in Deuteronomy, no doubt reflect a localized tendency to use כי to introduce statements of law of all

The few cases in which it is parallel to אם (as 2 Chron 7:13) probably represent late Aramaic influence. Waltke-O’Connor, #40.2.2d n. 26, are clearly right in rejecting אבי in 2 Kgs 5:13 as a conditional particle, as none is needed. This identification is speculative even in Job 34:36.
